title: Quran Study 67: Capital Punishment, Wills, Inheritance, and Adoption (1982-12-10)
date_note: Explicit in the filename. The recording directly continues Study 66.
source_file: data/sources/playlists/audio-transcripts/67 - Friday Sermon 10 Dec. 1982 By Dr. Rashad Khalifa.csv
document_summary: A direct continuation of the Quran 2:178–182 discussion. Rashad interprets equivalence in murder cases as a ceiling designed to spare lives rather than a command for execution, arguing that unlike categories shift a case toward compensation. He compares compensation with imprisonment, discusses victims or their kin as judges, wrongful execution, restitution, Quran 5:45, and the phrase 'life-saving law.' The group then studies wills, alteration of wills, correction of sinful partiality, Quranic inheritance shares, family obligations, gifts, charitable dependents, and whether adopted or non-Muslim children inherit. Dean Mahmoud describes Southeast Asian and Philippine practices that exclude adopted children or relatives of another religion, while Rashad rejects those restrictions as non-Quranic and says adopted children remain family members while retaining their lineage names.

sections.title: Quran 2:178–179, equivalence as a maximum, compensation, and sparing lives
sections.summary: Rashad rejects killing an innocent person of the same category and interprets the categories of free, enslaved, male, and female as excuses to avoid execution when killer and victim differ. The law sets a maximum of one life for one life, favors pardon and compensation, and is called life-saving.

sections.summary: Rashad says adopted children are members of the family and should receive equal treatment while retaining their original lineage names. He also rejects disinheriting children because they are Jewish, Christian, or otherwise outside the parent's religion. Dean describes Southeast Asian and Philippine customs excluding adopted children and interfaith relatives, a wealthy family fearing loss of an estate, and the possibility of transferring property as a lifetime gift.
